subtitle: Evacuation Decision & Vertical Critical-Care Moves

brief.userPrompt: Tuesday, September 15, 2026, a fictional hurricane, Quinlan, in the western Gulf. At 06:00 the National Hurricane Center advisory has Quinlan a Category 3 forecast to make landfall near Corpus Christi on Wednesday evening, with 34-knot winds forecast to reach the city at 18:00 Wednesday (H); the Nueces County Judge ordered Zone A evacuated at 04:00 and has not yet ordered Zone B, where Mariner Bay Medical Center sits, 1.4 miles from the bay with a storm surge forecast of 4 to 6 feet. The hospital's clearance time is 12 hours, so the horizontal evacuation decision is due by 06:00 Wednesday. The exercise starts at 06:00 Tuesday with the Hospital Incident Commander (COO Dennis Falcone) and CNO Dr. Marguerite Delacroix at the command center (ext. 4520), 12 NICU infants (3 on ventilators) and 19 ICU patients (6 ventilated) in house, 120 ride-out staff scheduled, and the fuel tanks filling. Pressure points: the shelter-or-evacuate decision against the NHC wind speed probabilities and the 12-hour clearance rule; the Transfer Center Liaison (Samira Haddad, ext. 4700) can find only 5 critical care ground ambulances and a helicopter that will stop flying at 34 knots, and the San Antonio hospitals are filling; a forecast shift at 07:00 Tuesday brings H forward by 6 hours; setting the evacuation priority order (ventilated infants and ventilated ICU patients first) when the Medical Director for Critical Care (Dr. Anil Chaudhary) and a family disagree about two infants; the staffing roster with 14 nurses short (the Staffing Coordinator, Rosalind Aguirre, has agency nurses who cannot cross the bridge) and a night with the NICU at 1:3 and ICU at 1:3 instead of 1:2; vertical evacuation Phase 1 at H minus 6 hours moving the NICU to 7 West and the ICU to 6 West in 90 minutes and 3 hours, with only 2 of 6 elevators on generator and a drill that last time took 74 minutes for 8 patients; an NICU infant on a ventilator whose early warning score jumps during the move; an ICU patient on 3 infusions whose pump battery fails on the stairs; two patients on contact isolation; a handoff to 7 West that leaves out an allergy and a pending culture; surge water on the ground floor at 20:00; the ED moved to the second floor; a disclosure conversation with a family within 60 minutes of a medication delay; a family member who refuses to leave the NICU; a post on social media that the hospital is evacuating all babies to Houston, which the PIO (Colin Reyes) must correct; staff who ask to leave to protect their own families. The SimCell plays the National Hurricane Center and NWS Corpus Christi, the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management and Judge, the Coastal Bend Regional Advisory Council, receiving hospitals in San Antonio and Victoria, the staffing agency, EMS and air transport, the electric utility, families and reporters.
constraints: Every email address of the hospital uses the exercise domain marinerbaymc.example; outside parties use fictional *.example domains; never a real hospital, staffing company or newspaper domain; phone numbers are 361-555-01xx.

Hurricane products follow the real National Hurricane Center format (advisory number, cone, wind speed probabilities, storm surge) and are marked as exercise products with the fictional storm name Quinlan; times are Central Daylight Time; no real storm's victims are depicted.

Patients are synthetic (bed and tag numbers or invented names); use the plan's ratios, 12-hour clearance rule and the 90-minute NICU and 3-hour ICU targets as written; player roles are only those in the audience list; the SimCell plays everyone else.

overview.theme: Deciding under a shrinking clock, keeping fragile patients safe when they have to move, and keeping trust with staff and families during a storm.
overview.threat: Hurricane Quinlan is a fictional Category 3 storm in the western Gulf. At 06:00 Tuesday, September 15, 2026, the exercise National Hurricane Center advisory forecasts landfall near Corpus Christi on Wednesday evening, with 34-knot winds (H) reaching the city at 18:00 Wednesday CDT and a storm surge of 4 to 6 feet. Before STARTEX, at 04:00, the Nueces County Judge ordered Zone A evacuated. Zone B, where Mariner Bay Medical Center sits 1.4 miles from the bay, has not been ordered out. Under the 12-hour clearance rule, the horizontal evacuation decision is due by 06:00 Wednesday. At 07:00 Tuesday a forecast shift moves H forward 6 hours, to 12:00 Wednesday. That moves the decision deadline to midnight Tuesday and Vertical Evacuation Phase 1 to 06:00 Wednesday. The causeways close and the road to San Antonio floods at its low points. After landfall, surge water reaches the ground floor at 20:00 Wednesday. The ground floor holds the ED, imaging and the main pharmacy, so the ED has to move to the second floor.
overview.operationalImpact: At STARTEX, the COO serving as Hospital Incident Commander and the CNO are in the command center (ext. 4520). In house are 12 NICU infants (3 on ventilators) and 19 ICU patients (6 ventilated). 120 ride-out staff are scheduled and the fuel tanks are filling. The Transfer Center Liaison (ext. 4700) can find only 5 critical care ground ambulances and one helicopter, which stops flying at 34 knots, and the San Antonio receiving hospitals are filling. The Medical Director for Critical Care and one family disagree about where two infants fall in the move order. The roster is 14 nurses short because the Staffing Coordinator's agency nurses cannot cross the bridge, which leaves the NICU and ICU at 1:3 instead of 1:2 on the night of landfall. Some staff ask to leave to protect their own families. During Phase 1, the NICU moves to 7 West (90-minute target) and the ICU to 6 West (3-hour target), with only 2 of 6 elevators on generator power. The last drill took 74 minutes for 8 patients. During the move, a ventilated NICU infant's early warning score jumps. An ICU patient's infusion pump battery fails on the stairs while the patient is on 3 infusions. Two contact-isolation patients need separate placement. A handoff to 7 West leaves out an allergy and a pending culture. A medication delay requires a disclosure conversation with the family within 60 minutes. One family member refuses to leave the NICU. A social media post claims all babies are being evacuated to Houston, and the PIO has to correct it. Families, reporters, the county, the Regional Advisory Council and the receiving hospitals call in throughout.

objectives.name: Decision Making
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to make and document the horizontal evacuation or shelter-in-place decision by the revised midnight Tuesday deadline after H moves to 12:00 Wednesday, weighing the NHC advisory, the Nueces County Judge's order, the 12-hour clearance rule, the 5 available critical care ground ambulances and the one helicopter, as set out in the Hurricane Plan sections 1 and 2.

objectives.name: Operational Coordination
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to carry out Vertical Evacuation Phase 1 at 06:00 Wednesday, moving the NICU to 7 West within 90 minutes and the ICU to 6 West within 3 hours using only the 2 elevators on generator power, while handling the infusion pump battery failure and keeping the two contact-isolation patients apart as NUR-EM-07 6 requires.

objectives.name: Patient Safety and Clinical Escalation
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to recognize and escalate the ventilated NICU infant's rising early warning score to a physician at the bedside within 15 minutes, catch and correct the missing allergy and pending culture in the 7 West handoff by structured read-back, and start the medication-delay disclosure conversation with the family within 60 minutes.

objectives.name: Communication
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to keep the CNO, the Transfer Center Liaison and the PIO on the same numbers (patients in house, patients transferred, staff on site, H), as Hurricane Plan 5 requires, and get a correction cleared and issued for the false post claiming that all babies are going to Houston.

roles.name: Incident Commander (Hospital Incident Commander / COO)
roles.team: Team A: Hospital Incident Commander / COO
roles.description: Owns the shelter-or-evacuate decision, the 6-hour operational period briefings in the command center (ext. 4520) and coordination with Nueces County OEM and the Regional Advisory Council.
standingOrders: Clock First: work back from H; the moment the forecast moves, reset the horizontal evacuation deadline to H minus 12 hours and announce it.
Decide on Record: make the evacuation decision with the CNO, the Medical Director for Critical Care, the Facilities Director and the county, not alone, and write down the reasons.
One Truth: clear every PIO statement yourself, and do not let reassurance get ahead of what the transfer center can deliver.

roles.name: Chief Nursing Officer (Operations Section Chief)
roles.description: Owns nursing operations, the vertical evacuation, ride-out staffing ratios and the shared census numbers.
standingOrders: Ratios Matter: escalate at once when the NICU or ICU drops to 1:3, and do not accept a ratio quietly to make the roster work.
Staff Are People: hear every request to leave, balance it against patient safety, and decide openly rather than by default.
Same Numbers: before any number goes to the PIO, check the census and transfer counts with the Transfer Center Liaison.

roles.name: House Supervisor (nursing supervisor)
roles.description: Manages the hourly unit status reports, cross-unit moves of staff and equipment, and the night-of-landfall leadership on the floor.
standingOrders: Hourly Pulse: collect census, acuity, staffing, supplies and equipment problems from every unit on the hour, and push problems up instead of absorbing them.
Elevator Discipline: give the 2 elevators on generator power to critical-care moves first and control the queue yourself.
Radio Fallback: if Wi-Fi drops, move to radio channel 3 at once and confirm that every unit can hear you.

roles.name: NICU Charge Nurse
roles.description: Leads the NICU move to 7 West within the 90-minute target, including the order of moves, hourly early warning scores and handoffs.
standingOrders: Watch the Baby: check early warning scores hourly for infants on respiratory support, and call a rapid response for a score of 7 or more even in the middle of a move.
Order of Move: follow the agreed move order and send disagreements about it to the Medical Director and the CNO, not the hallway.
Full Handoff: no infant leaves the unit until the receiving nurse on 7 West has read back allergies, lines and pending results.
Families to Liaison: refer media and social media questions to the PIO, and stay with a family that refuses to leave without letting them block the move.

roles.name: ICU Charge Nurse
roles.description: Leads the ICU move to 6 West within the 3-hour target, covering ventilated patients, infusions, isolation placement and the medication-delay disclosure.
standingOrders: Power Before Moving: check pump batteries and portable oxygen before every transport, and carry backup equipment on the stairs.
Isolation Holds: move contact-isolation patients by their own route to separate receiving rooms, and get the infection preventionist's approval before any cohort.
Disclose Promptly: start the conversation with the family about the medication delay within 60 minutes, with the facts you know.

roles.name: Transfer Center Liaison
roles.description: Owns the transfer center (ext. 4700): receiving hospital beds, ambulance and air assets, the level of care and mode for each patient, and the transfer counts.
standingOrders: Count Real Assets: report only confirmed ambulances, aircraft and receiving beds, and do not treat a promise as capacity.
Wind Limit: remember that air and ground transport stop at 34 knots, and tell the Incident Commander which transfers cannot finish before H.
Same Numbers: give the CNO and the PIO the same transferred and pending counts at every briefing.

phases.title: The Watch
phases.goal: Tests whether command reads an uncertain Hurricane Quinlan forecast correctly against the H-based timeline in Hurricane Plan section 1 and begins pre-positioning early: transfer capacity, ride-out staffing and fuel, while Zone B has no evacuation order yet.
beats: (06:00 Tue) SimCell delivers the exercise-marked National Hurricane Center advisory for Hurricane Quinlan (numbered advisory with cone, wind speed probabilities and storm surge graphic): Category 3, 34-knot winds (H) at Corpus Christi 18:00 Wed CDT, surge 4–6 ft. The Nueces County OEM daily call confirms the 04:00 Zone A order from the Nueces County Judge and says Zone B has no order. Players must state H, the 06:00 Wed horizontal evacuation deadline under the 12-hour clearance rule, and the actions now due at about H−36 h (visiting closed, ride-out teams report).

Transfer Center Liaison Samira Haddad (ext. 4700) reports what is available: 5 critical care ground ambulances and one helicopter that stops flying at 34 knots. San Antonio receiving hospitals are filling, so Victoria (about 90 miles) is the other option. The Coastal Bend Regional Advisory Council bed board shows few NICU beds. Transfer requests for the 3 ventilated NICU infants and 6 ventilated ICU patients must be decided on now.

Noise item: a routine Facilities note from Wesley Pruitt says the fuel tanks are filling toward 96-hour capacity, along with an unrelated linen vendor delivery-time query. It needs no decision and only tests whether the room stays on what matters.

The Staffing Coordinator reports the ride-out roster for the 120 staff is 14 nurses short because the agency nurses cannot cross the bridge. Two ICU nurses ask the House Supervisor by 'Storm Alert' text whether they can leave to protect their families. A NICU parent calls asking whether the unit is moving and whether they can stay.

The CNO and House Supervisor start the patient tracking board for 12 NICU infants and 19 ICU patients. The IC sets a common-numbers report (patients in house, patients transferred, staff on site, H) for the CNO, the Transfer Center Liaison and PIO Colin Reyes.

phases.title: The Clock Moves Up
phases.goal: Tests the exercise's one decision point. After the 07:00 forecast shift moves H to 12:00 Wednesday, command must make and document the horizontal-evacuate or shelter-in-place decision by the revised midnight deadline, weighing limited transport against surge risk.
beats: Time jump (07:00 Tue): an exercise-marked NHC advisory, followed by an NWS Corpus Christi (WFO CRP) hurricane local statement and Storm Surge Warning (exercise/test marked), moves H to 12:00 Wed. The horizontal evacuation deadline becomes 00:00 Tue night, and Vertical Evacuation Phase 1 under Hurricane Plan section 3 becomes due by 06:00 Wed. Players must re-brief the new H and record the change on the master tracking board.

Red herring (07:20): a staff member relays a report that the Nueces County Judge has ordered Zone B evacuated and the Harbor Bridge is already closed. A SimCell call to Nueces County OEM shows this is false: there is still no Zone B order. The hospital decides on patient evacuation independently either way.

DECISION POINT (by 00:00): the IC, CNO Dr. Marguerite Delacroix, Medical Director for Critical Care Dr. Anil Chaudhary, Facilities and Nueces County OEM must choose. Option one is to send the highest-risk patients out horizontally using 5 ground ambulances and one helicopter to San Antonio/Victoria before H, with the risk of a road transfer during the storm. Option two is to shelter in place and evacuate vertically, which means the ground floor ED, imaging and pharmacy are exposed to 4 ft of surge and the NICU and ICU run at 1:3 staffing. The decision is documented with its rationale.

Dr. Anil Chaudhary and a family disagree about where two NICU infants fall in the move order. The House Supervisor must apply the Evacuation Priority List in section 4: changes are made only by the Charge Nurse and attending as an exception with the reason recorded, and a family request needs House Supervisor approval.
The Coastal Bend RAC and a San Antonio receiving hospital call wanting a firm count of transfers by 23:00. The Transfer Center Liaison's count has to match the CNO's and the PIO's numbers.

phases.title: Vertical Evacuation Phase 1
phases.goal: Tests carrying out Vertical Evacuation Phase 1: NICU to 7 West within 90 minutes and ICU to 6 West within 3 hours on only 2 generator-powered elevators, while bedside escalation, equipment failure, isolation placement and structured handoff happen during the move.
beats: Time jump (08:00 Wed): the IC orders 'Vertical Evacuation, Phase 1' on radio channel 2. The NICU Charge Nurse starts moving infants from floor 2 to 7 West in priority order. Security holds 2 of the 6 elevators. The last drill moved 8 patients in 74 minutes, so the 90-minute target for 12 infants is at risk. Each move needs a provider order and an accepting receiving nurse. A NICU parent refuses to leave the bedside and the House Supervisor must manage it.

A ventilated NICU infant's early warning score jumps in the elevator lobby. The NICU Charge Nurse must recognize it, give an SBAR, and get a physician to the bedside within 15 minutes. The respiratory therapist assigned to the transport is needed in two places at once.

The ICU move to 6West begins (3-hour target). Because the elevators are backed up, an ICU patient on 3 infusions goes by stair chair, and the infusion pump battery fails in the stairwell. The four-person stairwell team and the ICU Charge Nurse must keep the infusions running and replace the pump.

Two contact-isolation ICU patients need separate rooms on 6 West, which is already full with 24 beds of portable telemetry. The ICU Charge Nurse and House Supervisor must place them apart as NUR-EM-07 requires without stalling the move.

The handoff for a 7 West NICU patient leaves out an allergy and a pending culture. A structured read-back (SBAR or I PASS the BATON) should catch and correct the omission. If it is missed, SimCell carries the error forward into Phase 4.

phases.title: Landfall and Return
phases.goal: Tests keeping patients safe and communication accurate through landfall and surge, then damage assessment, notifications and the plan's criteria for returning units to service.
beats: Time jump (12:00 Wed): H arrives and the helicopter is grounded. At 20:00, surge water reaches the ground floor. The ED moves to the second floor, the main pharmacy on the ground floor is cut off, and command moves to the Boardroom (floor 5, ext. 4520). Facilities sends a gauge or photo of water at the ED entrance.

Because the pharmacy is cut off, a scheduled dose for a 6West ICU patient is delayed and shows on the MAR. The CNO and ICU Charge Nurse must start the disclosure conversation with the family within 60 minutes and document it.

A social media post claims all Mariner Bay babies are being evacuated to Houston, and a reporter calls with a 30-minute deadline. PIO Colin Reyes needs the correction cleared by the IC using the common numbers from the CNO and Transfer Center Liaison, then posts it on the hospital website and through Nueces County OEM.

Hurdle: one of the two generator-powered elevators faults, and agency relief staff still cannot cross because the bridge and causeways remain closed. The 1:3 NICU/ICU staffing continues overnight, so the House Supervisor must reassign ride-out staff and decide whether to approve the staff release requests.

After winds stay below 34 knots for 2 hours: Facilities inspects the ground floor, and restoration priorities are set (ED, pharmacy, imaging). Notifications go to Nueces County OEM, TDEM via the State hospital coordination system, the Coastal Bend RAC and receiving hospitals. If any building damage forces a transfer, it follows NUR-EM-07 section 7 (report called in on ext. 4700). The phased return of NICU and ICU to floors 2 and 3 is planned, then ENDEX.

msel.event: Phone Call (OEM, 361-555-0122): "Mariner Bay, the state situation report closes at 23:00. I need your shelter-or-evacuate status and patient numbers before then. TxDOT expects to close the causeways and the US 181 bridge when tropical-storm winds arrive around noon. NWS says I-37 low points near the Nueces River could flood before that." Then Dr. Anil Chaudhary in the command center: "Of my 6 vented ICU patients, 4 can tolerate a 5.5-hour ground ride. Bed 3-07 is on 3 pressors and Bed 3-14 is proned, so neither should go. ICU charge, I need to know which of the 19 can move and how many contact-isolation patients we have. Beds 3-11 and 3-18 are on contact precautions with different organisms, so they can't share a rig or a room. Here's the trade: if we evacuate, vented patients ride 5.5 hours on 5 rigs and 2 helicopter missions into only 8 receiving beds. If we shelter, I'm running 1:3 on landfall night with the ED, imaging and pharmacy on a ground floor that sits under a 4 to 6 ft surge forecast."
msel.expectedAction: DECISION POINT: The IC decides with the CNO, the Medical Director, the Facilities Director and the county, and records the decision by the 00:00 deadline. The options are partial horizontal evacuation of transport-tolerant patients within the 8 confirmed beds, or shelter in place with Vertical Evacuation Phase 1 by 06:00. The costs are weighed openly: evacuating sends ventilated patients on 5.5-hour rides in 5 rigs and 2 helicopter missions into only 8 confirmed receiving beds; sheltering leaves 1:3 ratios on landfall night and the ED, imaging and pharmacy on a ground floor under a 4 to 6 ft surge forecast. The reasons go on record and the decision is reported to OEM before 23:00. The ICU Charge Nurse lists which patients can move and plans separate routes for the 2 isolation patients.

objectiveCapabilities.why: The Incident Commander must bring together the CNO, the Medical Director, the Facilities Director and Nueces County OEM. They make and record the shelter-or-evacuate decision by the revised midnight H−12 deadline under the Hurricane Plan timeline.
The decision depends on reading the NHC advisory, the wind probabilities, the Judge's zone order and the 12-hour clearance time correctly. It also depends on resetting H when the forecast shifts.
Players weigh the 5 critical care ground units and one helicopter, through the RAC and the transfer center, against the runs that can still finish before H.
Vertical Evacuation Phase 1 needs a timed IC order and coordinated NICU, ICU and House Supervisor actions to meet the 90-minute and 3-hour targets.
Moving the NICU to 7 West and the ICU to 6 West uses only the 2 generator-powered elevators, with stair chairs and sleds as backup. This is how patients are moved inside the building.

Players must recognize and escalate the infant's early warning score to a physician at the bedside within 15 minutes. They must also keep clinical continuity through the moves and disclose the medication delay within 60 minutes.
The PIO, the CNO and the Transfer Center Liaison must issue cleared statements that use the same numbers, and they must correct the false Houston post.
Consistent messages depend on one shared, current set of figures: patients in house, patients transferred, staff on site and H. The figures must be updated on the boards when the forecast changes.

hotwash.methodDescription: Ask the room for three things that went well and three things that broke or failed during the storm response. Go around the room one team at a time (command, nursing and critical care, transfer center, PIO, facilities), and write each item on the whiteboard under "Up" or "Down" before you move to the discussion questions.

questions.text: At 07:00 Tuesday, the forecast shift moved H to 12:00 Wednesday. That moved your horizontal evacuation deadline from 06:00 Wednesday to midnight Tuesday, and you lost six hours you thought you had. When did you stop trusting the original Hurricane Plan 1 timeline? Did you call the Nueces County OEM and NWS Corpus Christi before you decided, or after? Zone B had not been ordered out, and you had only 5 critical care ambulances and one helicopter. What fact, call or pre-set trigger would have let you make and document the shelter-or-evacuate decision sooner?

At I-14, the 6 West charge nurse told you she had 19 usable spaces. The intensivist then gave you the call on 3-07, who is on three pressors, and 3-14, who is proned, and asked for an answer before the 06:30 elevator slot. Did command understand the clinical risk of unproning a patient in a hallway? Did the clinicians understand the floor 3 problem: an isolated floor at 1:3 once the ground floor flooded? Who actually made that call? How did you keep 3-11 and 3-18 separate as NUR-EM-07 6 requires, and still fit the NICU move into 90 minutes and the ICU move into 3 hours on two generator-powered elevators?

In the middle of Vertical Evacuation Phase 1, the infusion pump battery failed and the ventilated NICU infant's early warning score kept rising. How long did it take to get a physician to the bedside, and what slowed it down? In the 7 West handoff, did you treat the structured read-back as real evidence and catch the missing allergy and the pending culture? Or was it a box you ticked to clear the elevator? Who started the medication-delay disclosure with the family, and was that inside 60 minutes?

At I-09, the Bay Tribune had a 21:00 deadline. At I-19, Coastal Bend 6 News was going live at 21:10. Both cited posts saying all the babies were going to Houston and that you were 14 nurses short. What did you tell the public before you knew the true numbers? Were the CNO, the Transfer Center Liaison and the PIO all working from the same count of patients in house, patients transferred, staff on site and H, as Hurricane Plan 5 requires? How long did it take to clear and issue a correction? Did those same numbers go into the status report the RAC wanted by 22:00 at I-21?

At I-04b, Dana asked to leave by noon to get her children out of Zone A. Luis, who is on the ride-out list, said his wife was 8 months pregnant in Flour Bluff. Everyone in the 'Storm Alert' group thread could see how you answered. What did you decide for each of them, and who decided it? How did your answer change ICU staffing once H moved forward six hours? Did the NICU and ICU rosters still keep a single-competency nurse in place, so that no off-unit nurse was ever left alone with a ventilated patient?

assumptions: The exercise is conducted in a no-fault learning environment: discussion is about Mariner Bay's plans, systems and decisions, not about grading individual nurses or leaders.
The scenario is plausible, and events occur as they are presented. Hurricane Quinlan, its advisories and all patients, families and posts are fictional but are treated as real for the length of play.

Players respond in accordance with existing plans, policies and procedures, including the Hurricane Plan (Emergency Operations Plan, Annex F). Where a plan is silent or unclear, players say what they would do and note the gap for the hot wash.
Players know only what has reached them through the module narrative and the injects. Information that would not reach the command center or the bedside at that time is not assumed.
Census, staffing, transport and bed numbers in the injects are the working numbers. Players reconcile them as they would on a real day and do not challenge them as exercise artifacts.
Clinical decisions are discussed at the level of escalation, communication and coordination. No real orders are written and no real patient care is changed.
artificialities: Time is compressed. Four one-hour modules represent about 39 hours of storm, with facilitator TIME JUMP cards at 07:00 Tuesday, 08:00 Wednesday and 09:00 Thursday (which replays the landfall night, 20:15 Wednesday). Actions between modules are assumed to have happened as the cards describe.

A Simulation Cell (SimCell) plays everyone outside the room: the National Hurricane Center and NWS Corpus Christi, the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, the Coastal Bend RAC and receiving hospitals, Gulf Coast Critical Transport, Coastal AirCare 2, Gulf Nurse Staffing, the Facilities Director, the Medical Director for Critical Care, the PIO, the pharmacist, staff, families, reporters and social media users.

Systems named in the plans are talked through but not used. This includes the Storm Alert text group, radio channels 2 and 3, the satellite phones, the patient tracking boards, the elevators, the transfer center (ext. 4700), the hospital website and the state hospital coordination system. No real calls, posts, pages or patient moves are made.
Injects arrive on paper cards or on screen and are read aloud by the facilitator. Advisories, emails, radio calls and social media posts are mock-ups marked EXERCISE.
Telephone numbers, email addresses and patient names in the materials are exercise placeholders. Players do not dial or message them.

**Module 1: The Watch. 06:00 to about 07:00, Tuesday, September 15, 2026**

It is 06:00 CDT. Hurricane Quinlan is a Category 3 hurricane in the western Gulf. In Corpus Christi it is overcast and 84°F, with wind from the southeast at 12 mph gusting to 20, showers coming off the bay and seas building. Mariner Bay Medical Center is in normal operations, with 268 of 310 beds filled. The NICU on floor 2 has 12 infants, 3 of them on ventilators. The ICU on floor 3 has 19 patients, 6 of them ventilated. The ED has an ordinary weekday volume.

COO Dennis Falcone, acting as Hospital Incident Commander, and CNO Dr. Marguerite Delacroix are in the command center. The ride-out roster lists 120 staff, and the fuel tanks are being filled. There is no evacuation order for Zone B. The 06:00 daily call with Nueces County OEM is about to begin, and the first new NHC advisory of the day is expected on it.

Starting transfer requests and pre-positioning before Zone B has any evacuation order
Ride-out staffing gaps in critical care that fall against staff members' own family evacuations
Answering the county's "shelter or evacuate?" question before the hospital has decided

**Module 2: The Clock Moves Up. 07:00 Tuesday to 00:00 Wednesday, September 15–16, 2026**

It is 07:00 CDT on Tuesday. At 04:00 the advisory placed Corpus Christi under a hurricane warning with 4 to 6 ft of surge. The Judge ordered Zone A out, contraflow began on US 181, and Zone B received no order. The RAC confirmed 5 critical care ground units and one helicopter for Mariner Bay and reported only a few NICU and adult ventilator beds in San Antonio and Victoria. The San Antonio round trip is about 5.5 hours. The 14 agency RNs remain stuck in Portland, so the ICU will run at 1:3 and most NICU infants at 1:3. Staff have asked to leave to evacuate their families, and NICU parents are asking about a post that says all babies are going to Houston.

The 16:00 advisory says Quinlan is speeding up. It now has 120 mph winds, and tropical-storm-force winds are expected near Corpus Christi around **12:00 Wednesday**, about 6 hours earlier than forecast. The 34 kt wind probability is 94%. NWS Corpus Christi warns that roads to the causeways and the low points on I-37 may flood before the strongest winds arrive. **H is now 12:00 Wednesday.** The final horizontal evacuation order deadline is **00:00 tonight**, 7 hours from now, and Vertical Evacuation Phase 1 is due by 06:00. The census has not changed: 12 NICU infants (3 ventilated) and 19 ICU patients (6 ventilated). Rain bands are reaching the bay, with gusts to 30 mph.
keyIssues: The single decision point: order horizontal evacuation (for some or all patients) or shelter in place, and document it before 00:00
Too few transport runs and receiving beds compared with the number of critical patients and the surge risk at a ground floor in Zone B
Prioritizing patients by clinical need under pressure from families and the hospital president's office
Rumors (a Zone B order, bridge closures, babies to Houston) while the numbers have to be checked
A firm count is due to the RAC by 23:00 and a status to the state situation report by 23:00

modules.narrativeMd:
**Module 3: Vertical Evacuation Phase 1. 08:00 to about 09:00, Wednesday, September 16, 2026**

It is 08:00 CDT on Wednesday. Overnight the hospital moved to shelter in place. Ground transfers have stopped, Coastal AirCare 2 flew its last mission at 03:40, and contraflow on US 181 has ended. Heavy rain bands are crossing the city with gusts to 45 mph, and water is already ponding on Ocean Drive. H is still 12:00 today.

At 08:00 on radio channel 2 the Incident Commander announced: "Vertical Evacuation, Phase 1, is in effect. NICU to 7 West now. ICU to 6 West when NICU has elevator priority cleared." Security holds the 2 elevators on generator power for patient movement only, and the other 4 are locked out in the lobby. In house are 12 NICU infants (3 ventilated) on floor 2 and 19 ICU patients (6 ventilated) on floor 3, reduced by any patients sent out overnight. The ICU is at 1:3. The NICU target is 07:00. In last April's drill, 8 ICU patients moved in 74 minutes, a pace at which 12 infants would take about 111 minutes. Every move needs a provider order and a receiving nurse who has accepted the patient by name and bed.
keyIssues: Meeting the 90-minute NICU and 3-hour ICU targets with only two elevators and the drill pace showing it will be late
Keeping the bedside alert to deterioration while patients are moving
Limited respiratory therapists, transport ventilators and power for equipment during the move
Placing patients on 6 West when there are only two private rooms and two contact-isolation patients
Structured handoff to cross-trained receiving nurses, and families present at the bedside during the move

**Module 4: Landfall and Return. 20:15 to 21:30, Wednesday, September 16, 2026**

It is 20:15 CDT on Wednesday. Tropical-storm-force winds reached Corpus Christi at 12:00. Coastal AirCare 2 is grounded, and the causeways and the US 181 bridge are closed. Quinlan made landfall at 15:40 as a Category 3 just south of the city. At 20:00 surge water came in under the ED ambulance doors. The ED is moving its patients and crash carts to the second floor, and the ground floor pharmacy and imaging are cut off. The command center has moved to the Boardroom on floor 5 (ext. 4520).

The NICU (12 infants) is on 7 West and the ICU is on 6 West, reflecting this morning's placement decisions. Both are at 1:3, except for 1:1 nursing for the ventilated infants. At 20:11 the Facilities Director texted a gauge photo: water at the ED entrance is at 18 inches and rising about 3 inches every 20 minutes, and the pharmacy door sill is under water. The generators on the second floor mezzanine are dry and carrying full load with fuel at 81%. Gusts outside are 85 mph.

Telling a family about a delayed dose openly and on time
Correcting a viral false post about the NICU before a live broadcast deadline
Losing elevator capacity and staff with 1:3 ratios and no relief nurses coming
Reporting status after landfall, assessing damage, and applying the plan's criteria for returning units
